subject: How to deal with missing data in spatial models?

messages.author: 461a0c7d7557dffc
messages.subject: How to deal with missing data in spatial models?
parts:
Dear list,

I'm starting discovering INLA capabilities with simple spatial models and already stumbled upon a problem.

I'm working with individual level data of my study population (120k individuals) distributed over 3000+ spatial units (post code areas).
Each individual has a binary outcome indicating their obesity status, as well as continuous outcome (BMI). Using this data I'm fitting simple binomial and gausian models with 'besag' regional components.

Approximately 100 postcodes have no observation whatsoever. These are legitimate missings since they are located in very sparsely or unpopulated areas.

My question is - how to deal with situation like that?

Shall I compute the graph using all postal code and feed it into inla call? What is happening to the areas where there are no observations?
Or alternatively - shall I compute the graph excluding areas with no observations (changing the structure of 'original' graph with all postal codes of the country)?

radek

messages.author: 66ed4f72a898a51c
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to deal with missing data in spatial models?
parts:
There is no limitation with some missing observations. But, this seems a
case with may can be better to work with a graph without that areas.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to deal with missing data in spatial models?
parts:
On 3 February 2014 14:38, Daniel Simpson <dp.si...@gmail.com> wrote:
> If you include these areas, you will get predictions based on nearby
> observations, however the posterior variance will be much higher than the
> areas in which you observed counts.

Note:
1) How much higher the variances will be depends on the model.
2) This is not a problem in any way; it simply reflects the lack of
data at that location.

I would recommend using the full graph to build the model, since the
unobserved values do exist, you just don't have them, and changing the
model of world because of that is philosophically awkward.

Finn

Dear All,

I'm once again working on the models and this time I incorporated Finn's suggestion to use the graph build from all spatial units (including those with no observations).

The model provides me with structured component for all spatial units, and unstructured component - for spatial units where I have observations.

Two questions:

1) Are such results expected?

2) Does it make sense to include one 'dummy' observation per each spatial unit where number of cases and Ntrials (I'm working with binomial model) are both set to NAs?

Radek

On 5 Apr 2014, at 16:45, Radoslaw Panczak <r.pa...@gmail.com> wrote:
I'm once again working on the models and this time I incorporated Finn's suggestion to use the graph build from all spatial units (including those with no observations).

The model provides me with structured component for all spatial units, and unstructured component - for spatial units where I have observations.

Two questions:

1) Are such results expected?
Yes.
2) Does it make sense to include one 'dummy' observation per each spatial unit where number of cases and Ntrials (I'm working with binomial model) are both set to NAs?

If you want to compute the posteriors for the predictor for all locations, yes, that cane done by supplying NA for those locations.  (Ntrials does to affect the link function, but I'm not sure if you need to set it to an NA-value anyway).  See the r-inla.org FAQ entry about making postior predictions.

Finn

Radek
